questions.q: Is Brightfield Agritech, the company in this case study, a real business?
options: No — it's explicitly described as a fictional, illustrative composite scenario
Yes — it is a real, named precision-agriculture company
Yes — it is a real company whose name was changed for privacy
The lesson does not say whether it is real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Brightfield Agritech as fictional and illustrative, consistent with this catalog's policy against presenting invented scenarios as real.

questions.q: What did the stakeholder analysis in Chapter 1's application reveal was the actual root cause of Brightfield's data disagreements?
options: A field-equipment vendor's data format, not either internal team
A deliberate decision by the finance team to falsify numbers
A complete absence of any data at all
A disagreement that had no identifiable cause
questions.explain: The stakeholder analysis surfaced the vendor's data format as the real root inconsistency, ahead of either internal team being individually at fault.

questions.q: Why did Brightfield's adoption effort nearly stall, per this lesson's application of Chapter 4?
options: Field agronomists saw the new workflow as added friction to their fieldwork, with no new policy fixing that by itself
The governance council wrote no policy at all
There were no KPIs or dashboards of any kind
The company had no governance charter
questions.explain: The problem was adoption among people doing daily field work, not a gap in policy, measurement, or charter — which is why the fix was communication and peer-led training, not a new rule.

questions.q: How did Brightfield's maturity assessment (Chapter 5) connect to its Chapter 4 adoption struggle?
options: The assessment scored adoption outside the pilot team as only 'developing,' matching the real struggle almost exactly
The maturity assessment found no relationship to adoption at all
The assessment replaced the need for any KPIs
The assessment was conducted before the program existed
questions.explain: The maturity assessment surfacing a weak adoption dimension is presented as the assessment correctly doing its job — confirming a problem the team had already been living with.

questions.q: How was Brightfield's budget defended during the company-wide cost review, per this lesson?
options: With a value realization report leading with the dispute-rate drop and resolution-time improvement, framed for the CFO as rework and risk avoided
By asking the CFO to simply trust the program without evidence
By canceling the governance council entirely to save money
The budget was cut and the program was shut down
questions.explain: The lesson ties Lesson 22's value realization report directly to the successful budget defense, framed specifically for the CFO's concerns.
